course: Cosmetics: Lip Balms, Body Butters & Hair Oils

lessons.title: Basic Lip Balm Recipe with Shea Butter and Beeswax
lessons.body: To make a basic lip balm, you need three main ingredients: shea butter, beeswax, and a carrier oil. A simple recipe by weight is 30% shea butter, 30% beeswax, and 40% carrier oil. For a small batch, use 30g shea butter, 30g beeswax, and 40g oil. Good carrier oils in Africa include coconut oil, baobab oil, moringa oil, or sunflower oil. You will also need a double boiler (or a small pot with a heat-proof bowl), a kitchen scale, a spoon for stirring, and lip balm tubes or tins. First, sanitize all tools and containers with hot water and soap, then dry them. Weigh the beeswax and shea butter into the top of the double boiler. Melt them over low heat, stirring gently until fully liquid. Add the carrier oil and stir until combined. Remove from heat. If you want a firmer balm, add 5g more beeswax; for a softer balm, add 5g more oil. Carefully pour the hot mixture into your tubes or tins. Fill them to the top because the balm shrinks as it cools. Let them sit undisturbed for 1-2 hours until completely solid. This recipe makes about 100g of balm, enough for 10 standard 10ml tubes. Always test on a small area of your skin before using on lips. Store in a cool, dark place. In hot climates, keep beeswax at 35% to prevent melting. This basic recipe is your foundation; you can adjust it later for different skin needs.

lessons.title: Adding Flavor and Scent with Local Herbs and Fruits
lessons.body: Flavor and scent make your lip balm enjoyable and can also provide therapeutic benefits. In Africa, you have access to many local herbs and fruits. For flavor, you can use food-grade essential oils or extracts. Common choices: peppermint oil (cooling), citrus oils like orange or lemon (refreshing), and vanilla extract (sweet). For scent, you can infuse your carrier oil with dried herbs or fruit peels. To make an infusion, gently heat 50g of carrier oil with 10g of dried herb (like rosemary, mint, or hibiscus) in a double boiler for 30 minutes. Strain out the herbs. Use this infused oil in your basic recipe. Be careful with fresh fruits because they contain water, which can cause mold. Instead, use dried fruit peels or zest. For a fruity scent, add 1-2 drops of food-grade fruit flavor oil per 10g of balm. Always add flavors and scents after you remove the melted mixture from heat, because heat can destroy the aroma. A good rule: 1-2% of total weight. For 100g batch, use 1-2g (about 20-40 drops) of essential oil or flavor. Mix well. Test the scent by smelling the cooled balm; if too weak, you can add more, but never exceed 3% because essential oils can irritate lips. Popular African combinations: mint and baobab, hibiscus and shea, and lemon and moringa. Remember, some essential oils like citrus are photosensitive, so avoid sun exposure after applying. Label your balms with the flavor and date. Store away from heat to preserve scent.

lessons.title: Using Natural Colorants like Beetroot and Alkanet
lessons.body: Natural colorants give your lip balm a subtle tint without synthetic dyes. Beetroot powder and alkanet root are easy to find in African markets. Beetroot gives a pink to red color. Alkanet root gives a deep red to purple. To use beetroot, dry fresh beetroot slices in the sun or oven, then grind into a fine powder. For alkanet, buy dried alkanet root and grind it. You can add color in two ways: infuse your carrier oil or add powder directly. For oil infusion: mix 10g of dried colorant with 100g of carrier oil. Heat gently in a double boiler for 1-2 hours, stirring occasionally. Strain through a fine cloth. The oil will take on the color. Use this colored oil in your basic recipe. For direct powder: add 1-2g of finely ground powder to your melted balm mixture. Stir well and pour. Be careful: too much powder makes the balm gritty. Start with 0.5g per 100g and adjust. Beetroot powder may fade over time, so store in dark containers. Alkanet is more stable. You can also combine colorants for different shades. For a brick red, mix beetroot and alkanet. For a soft pink, use only beetroot. Test the color by putting a small drop on white paper; the color will be lighter on lips. Always label the colorant used. Natural colorants are safe for lips, but do a patch test if you have sensitive skin. Avoid using synthetic food dyes as they may contain harmful chemicals.

lessons.title: Testing Lip Balm for Stability and Texture
lessons.body: After making your lip balm, you must test it for stability and texture. Stability means it doesn't melt, separate, or go rancid quickly. Texture means it feels smooth, not grainy, and glides on lips. Start with a small batch of 50g. Pour into 5 tubes. Let them cool for 24 hours. Then do these tests: First, the heat test. Put one tube in a warm place (like a car in the sun or near a stove) at about 40Â°C for 2 hours. If it melts completely, your balm is too soft. Increase beeswax by 5% next time. If it stays firm, good. Second, the cold test. Put one tube in a refrigerator at 4Â°C for 2 hours. It should not crack. If it cracks, you have too much wax; reduce by 5%. Third, the texture test. Rub a small amount on your lips. It should feel smooth, not gritty. If gritty, your shea butter or beeswax may not have melted fully, or you added powder too quickly. Re-melt and stir more. Fourth, the stability test. Keep a tube at room temperature for 4 weeks. Check for separation (oil pooling on top) or rancid smell. If oil separates, your emulsification was poor; re-melt and add 1g of beeswax per 50g. If rancid, your oil was old or you didn't use enough vitamin E (add 0.5% vitamin E oil as an antioxidant). Fifth, the shelf life test. Write the date on a tube and check monthly for 3 months. Most natural balms last 6-12 months. Record all results in a notebook. Adjust your recipe based on findings. This testing ensures your product is consistent and safe for sale.

lessons.title: Filling and Labeling Lip Balm Tubes and Tins
lessons.body: Filling and labeling are crucial for professional-looking lip balms. You need clean, dry containers. Common containers: plastic tubes (5ml, 10ml), metal tins (15ml, 30ml), and glass jars. For tubes, use a pipette or a small funnel. Hold the tube upright. Pour the melted balm slowly to avoid air bubbles. Fill to the top because it shrinks when cooling. For tins, pour until the balm reaches the rim. Let them cool undisturbed for 1-2 hours. Do not move them. After cooling, wipe any spills with a clean cloth. For labeling, you need waterproof labels or sticker paper. Include: product name, ingredients, weight, your business name, and contact. Also add a batch number and date made. For example: 'Shea Mint Lip Balm, 10ml, Made 15/06/2025, Batch 001'. Use a laser or inkjet printer for labels. If no printer, write neatly with a permanent marker. For a professional look, use a round label for tins and a rectangular label for tubes. You can also add a shrink band around the cap for tamper evidence. In Africa, you can buy labels from local print shops or order online. Always label before selling. Store filled balms in a cool, dark place. For transport, pack in a box with cushioning to prevent melting. If selling at markets, keep a cooler box. Proper filling and labeling build trust and make your product stand out.

lessons.title: Creating Lip Balm Variants for Different Skin Needs
lessons.body: Different people have different lip needs. You can create variants by adjusting your base recipe. For dry, cracked lips: increase shea butter to 40%, reduce beeswax to 25%, and add 5% cocoa butter. Add 1% vitamin E oil. This gives deep moisture. For sensitive or allergy-prone lips: use only shea butter, beeswax, and jojoba oil. Avoid essential oils and colorants. Add 2% colloidal oatmeal for soothing. For cold sore prone lips: add 2% lemon balm extract or 1% tea tree oil (but tea tree can irritate, so use sparingly). For sun protection: add 5% zinc oxide (non-nano) and 2% raspberry seed oil (natural SPF). Note: this is not a replacement for sunscreen. For tinted lips: add beetroot or alkanet as in Lesson 3. For glossy finish: replace 10% of beeswax with candelilla wax and add 5% castor oil. For men: use unscented, matte finish with 40% beeswax, 30% shea, 30% coconut oil. For children: use edible ingredients only, no essential oils, and add 1% honey (but honey can be sticky). Always test each variant for stability. Label clearly: 'For Dry Lips', 'Sensitive', etc. You can sell a variety pack. In Africa, popular variants include baobab oil for repair, moringa for anti-aging, and hibiscus for color. Keep records of each recipe. Adjust based on customer feedback. This is how you build a product line.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Lip Balm Formulation, Testing & Production in the African Context

This Practical Reference consolidates the core technical knowledge from the six lessons in the Lip Balm Formulation and Production module. It is written for African agribusiness entrepreneurs who want to move from kitchen-scale experimentation to consistent, market-ready production. Whether you are sourcing shea butter from northern Ghana, beeswax from Tanzania, or alkanet root from the Sahel, the principles below will help you standardise your craft, reduce waste, and build a brand that buyers trust.

Lip balm is one of the lowest-barrier entry points in cosmetics manufacturing: the equipment is simple, the raw materials are largely available across the continent, and the margins can be healthy when you control quality. But the market punishes inconsistency. A batch that separates in the heat, smells rancid after two months, or stains the lips unevenly will cost you repeat customers. This reference gives you the numbers, checks, and sourcing logic to avoid those failures.

1. The Base Formula: Getting Ratios Right

Every reliable lip balm starts with three functional components: a wax for structure, a butter for emollience and occlusivity, and a liquid carrier oil for glide and spread. In the African context, the default trio is unrefined shea butter (Vitellaria paradoxa), local beeswax, and a carrier oil such as baobab, moringa, or coconut. The wax-to-butter-to-oil ratio determines whether your balm is hard, soft, grainy, or stable in heat.

Unrefined shea butter has a melting point around 32â35 Â°C and is rich in stearic and oleic acids, giving it excellent skin feel but a tendency to become grainy if heated too high or cooled too fast. Beeswax melts at 62â65 Â°C and provides the structural backbone. A common starting ratio by weight is 1 part beeswax : 2 parts shea butter : 2 parts carrier oil. For a firmer balm for hot climates, shift to 1.2 : 2 : 1.8; for a softer balm for dry harmattan conditions, use 0.8 : 2.2 : 2.

Table 1: Starter formulation ratios for African-sourced lip balm (by weight, 100 g batch)
Ingredient Function Firm / Hot Climate Balanced Soft / Dry Climate
Beeswax (local) Structure, occlusivity 30 g 25 g 20 g
Unrefined shea butter Emollient, film former 40 g 40 g 45 g
Carrier oil (baobab/moringa/coconut) Glide, spreadability 25 g 30 g 30 g
Vitamin E (tocopherol) Antioxidant 1 g 1 g 1 g
Flavour / essential oil Scent, taste 2â3 g 2â3 g 2â3 g
Natural colourant Tint 0.5â2 g 0.5â2 g 0.5â2 g

Source: Ratios adapted from Ilesanmi et al. (2020), J. Cosmet. Dermatol. Sci. Appl., 10(2), and standard shea butterâbeeswax balm practice documented by the Global Shea Alliance formulation guides.

2. Flavour, Scent and Colour from Local Botanicals

Flavour and scent are where African producers can differentiate. Instead of imported synthetic flavours, consider hibiscus (tart, slightly astringent), moringa leaf (grassy, nutrient-rich), baobab fruit powder (citrusy), ginger (warming), and lemongrass (fresh, antimicrobial). For scent, steam-distilled essential oils from local producers â e.g., Cymbopogon citratus (lemongrass), Ocimum gratissimum (African basil), and Pelargonium graveolens (rose geranium) â work well at 0.5â2% of total weight.

Natural colourants: beetroot powder gives a soft pink-red at 0.5â1.5%; alkanet root (Alkanna tinctoria) gives a deep ruby at 0.5â2%; annatto gives orange; cocoa powder gives brown. Always disperse colourants in a small amount of warm carrier oil before adding to the melt â this prevents speckling. Note that beetroot colour fades with light and heat; alkanet is more stable but can stain. Label accordingly.

Table 2: Common African botanical additives â usage rates, function and stability
Botanical Part used Usage rate Function Stability note
Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa) Dried calyx powder 0.5â2% Colour, tart flavour Fades in light; store dark
Beetroot (Beta vulgaris) Powder 0.5â1.5% Pink-red tint Heat-sensitive; add below 45 Â°C
Alkanet (Alkanna tinctoria) Root infused oil 0.5â2% Ruby tint Stable; can stain fabric
Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) Essential oil 0.5â1% Scent, antimicrobial Use within 12 months
Baobab (Adansonia digitata) Fruit powder / seed oil 1â3% Flavour, vitamin C Keep dry; oil stable 18 months
Moringa (Moringa oleifera) Leaf powder / seed oil 0.5â2% Nutrient claim, green tint Colour fades; oil stable

Source: Usage rates compiled from Ilesanmi et al. (2020); FAO (2022) Non-wood forest products and African botanical value chains; and Global Shea Alliance (2021) Shea Butter Formulation Guidelines.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Read before every batch

Never heat waxes or oils over an open flame or unattended. Beeswax and carrier oils are flammable when overheated; use a water bath or double boiler and keep a lid or fire blanket within reach. Do not exceed 80 Â°C. Essential oils are concentrated: never exceed 2% of total weight in a leave-on lip product, and avoid citrus oils that are phototoxic. Do not use essential oils known to irritate mucous membranes (e.g., cinnamon, clove, oregano) above 0.1%. If you sell in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, or South Africa, check national cosmetic regulations â KEBS, NAFDAC, FDA Ghana, and SAHPRA require ingredient labelling, batch numbers, and in some cases product notification. Keep a Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) for every input, and never reuse containers that held non-food chemicals.

3. Stability and Texture Testing

Before you fill 500 tubes, run a small batch through a stability protocol. The goal is to predict how your balm behaves in real African conditions: 35â45 Â°C ambient heat, harmattan dryness, and humidity swings. Minimum tests:

  • Heat test: Place a filled tube at 45 Â°C for 48 hours. It should not leak, sweat oil, or collapse. If it does, increase beeswax by 2â5%.
  • Cool test: Place at 4 Â°C for 24 hours, then return to room temperature. Check for graininess or wax bloom.
  • Drop test: Drop a tube from 1 m onto a hard floor three times. The balm should not crack or detach from the tube.
  • Texture panel: Have 5â10 people rate glide, greasiness, waxiness, and after-feel on a 1â5 scale. Aim for glide â¥4 and waxiness â¤2.
  • Accelerated ageing: Keep one sample at 40 Â°C for 4 weeks. Check for rancidity (smell), colour shift, and separation. If rancid, increase vitamin E or switch to a more stable carrier oil.

4. Filling, Labelling and Variants

Fill at 55â60 Â°C â too hot and you melt the tube; too cool and the balm sets before filling. For 5 g tubes, a simple jug with a spout or a large syringe works. Tap tubes gently to remove air bubbles. Cap immediately and allow to set undisturbed for 2 hours. Label with: product name, net weight, full ingredient list (INCI or common names), batch code, manufacture date, best-before date, and your business contact. In many African markets, a barcode and country of manufacture are also required for retail.

Variants for different needs: Healing (add 1% calendula-infused oil), Sun protection (add 5â10% zinc oxide â note this becomes a cosmetic with SPF claims, so check regulations), Overnight mask (higher shea, lower wax), Men's (unscented, matte, higher wax), Kids (no essential oils, food-grade flavour only). Each variant should have its own batch code and stability record.

â Quick Reference Checklist â Before You Sell

  1. Weigh every ingredient on a calibrated scale (Â±0.1 g); record the batch.
  2. Melt in a water bath, never over open flame; keep below 80 Â°C.
  3. Add flavour, colour and vitamin E below 50 Â°C to protect actives.
  4. Run a 48-hour heat test at 45 Â°C and a 4-week accelerated ageing test.
  5. Check texture with at least 5 testers; aim for glide â¥4, waxiness â¤2.
  6. Fill at 55â60 Â°C; cap and set for 2 hours before labelling.
  7. Label with ingredients, net weight, batch code, dates and contact.
  8. Keep an MSDS and a batch record for every production run; check national regulations (KEBS, NAFDAC, FDA Ghana, SAHPRA).

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Non-wood forest products and African botanical value chains (PDF) â sourcing and sustainability of shea, baobab and moringa.
  • Global Shea Alliance â Formulation and Quality Guidelines â shea butter handling, grades and cosmetic use.
  • WHO â Guidelines on good manufacturing practices for cosmetics â GMP principles applicable to small workshops.
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â cosmetic labelling and standards for East African markets.
  • NAFDAC Nigeria â Cosmetics Registration Guidelines â product notification and labelling requirements.

This Practical Reference is part of the Rise Africa Skills course Cosmetics: Lip Balms, Body Butters & Hair Oils. Always verify current national regulations before commercial sale.

quiz.q: What are the three main ingredients in a basic lip balm recipe?
options: A) Shea butter, beeswax, carrier oil
B) Coconut oil, cocoa butter, vitamin E
quiz.explanation: The basic recipe uses shea butter, beeswax, and a carrier oil.

quiz.q: What is the recommended percentage of beeswax in a basic lip balm for a firmer balm?
quiz.explanation: The basic recipe uses 30% beeswax, and increasing it makes a firmer balm.

quiz.q: Why should you fill lip balm tubes to the top?
options: B) Because the balm shrinks when cooling
C) To make it look full
quiz.explanation: The balm shrinks as it solidifies, so filling to the top ensures a full tube.

quiz.q: Which carrier oil is NOT commonly used in African lip balm recipes?
quiz.explanation: Olive oil is not typically highlighted in African recipes; baobab, moringa, and sunflower are common.

quiz.q: How long should you let the lip balm sit undisturbed after pouring?
quiz.explanation: The balm needs 1-2 hours to cool and solidify completely.

quiz.q: What is a safe maximum percentage for essential oils in lip balm?
quiz.explanation: Essential oils should not exceed 3% to avoid irritation.

quiz.q: Which local herb is commonly used for a cooling flavor in lip balm?
quiz.explanation: Mint provides a cooling sensation and is a popular flavor.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using fresh fruits in lip balm?
options: B) They contain water that can cause mold
quiz.explanation: Fresh fruits contain water, which promotes mold growth in the balm.

quiz.q: How do you make an herbal oil infusion for lip balm?
options: A) Mix herbs with cold oil and let sit for a week
B) Heat oil and herbs in a double boiler for 30 minutes
C) Blend herbs with oil in a blender
D) Add herbs directly to melted balm
quiz.explanation: Gentle heating in a double boiler extracts the herbs' properties.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of flavor oil per 10g of balm?
quiz.explanation: 1-2 drops of flavor oil is sufficient for 10g of balm.

quiz.q: Which natural colorant gives a deep red to purple color?
quiz.explanation: Alkanet root is known for its deep red to purple hue.

quiz.q: What is the first step to prepare beetroot for use as a colorant?
options: B) Dry and grind into powder
quiz.explanation: Drying and grinding beetroot creates a fine powder for coloring.

quiz.q: How much colorant powder should you start with per 100g of balm?
quiz.explanation: Start with 0.5g to avoid grittiness and adjust as needed.

quiz.q: Which colorant is more stable over time?
quiz.explanation: Alkanet is more stable and less likely to fade than beetroot.

quiz.q: What does a heat test on lip balm determine?
quiz.explanation: The heat test checks if the balm melts at high temperatures.

quiz.q: If your lip balm cracks after being in the refrigerator, what should you adjust?
quiz.explanation: Cracking indicates too much wax, so reduce beeswax.

quiz.q: What does oil pooling on top of a lip balm indicate?
quiz.explanation: Oil separation means the ingredients didn't bind well.

quiz.q: How much vitamin E oil can you add as an antioxidant?
quiz.explanation: 0.5% vitamin E oil helps prevent rancidity.

quiz.q: How long should you test a lip balm at room temperature for stability?
quiz.explanation: A 4-week test reveals separation or rancidity.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a batch number on a label?
quiz.explanation: Batch numbers help trace when the product was made.

quiz.q: Which container is best for a solid lip balm?
quiz.explanation: Tubes, tins, and jars are all suitable for lip balm.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after filling a lip balm tube?
options: D) Put it in the fridge
quiz.explanation: The balm must cool and solidify without disturbance.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label your lip balm with ingredients?
options: B) To inform customers with allergies
C) To make it look professional
quiz.explanation: Ingredient labels are required for safety, legal, and professional reasons.

quiz.q: What is a good label size for a 10ml lip balm tube?
quiz.explanation: A 2cm x 5cm label fits well on a standard tube.

quiz.q: For dry, cracked lips, which ingredient should you increase?
quiz.explanation: Increasing shea butter provides more moisture.

quiz.q: Which variant is best for sensitive lips?
options: C) One with only shea, beeswax, and jojoba
D) One with tea tree oil
quiz.explanation: Sensitive lips need minimal ingredients without potential irritants.

quiz.q: What natural ingredient can provide sun protection in lip balm?
quiz.explanation: Zinc oxide is a natural mineral sunscreen.

quiz.q: Which wax can be used to make a glossier lip balm?
quiz.explanation: Candelilla wax gives a glossy finish when substituted for some beeswax.

quiz.q: What should you avoid when making lip balm for children?
quiz.explanation: Essential oils can be too strong for children's sensitive skin.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of your lip balm recipes?
options: B) To adjust for customer feedback
quiz.explanation: Records help you reproduce, improve, and maintain quality.
